title: Simplicial enriched localization and homotopy-limit comparison calculus
statement:
Use simplicial model categories and combinatorial projective models as in [lem-coef-simplicial-projective-model-calculus], and small simplicial categories as in [lem-coef-simplicial-interval-lifting]. Enlarge universes so all categories under discussion are small. A Dwyer--Kan equivalence is an enriched functor inducing weak homotopy equivalences on mapping sets and an equivalence on their path-component categories. Homotopy limits and homotopy pushouts of simplicial categories below mean derived limits and colimits for the Dwyer--Kan model structure: weak equivalences are Dwyer--Kan equivalences, fibrant categories have Kan mapping sets, and fibrations between fibrant categories are local Kan fibrations with the lifting property for isomorphisms of path-component categories. For a simplicial category $C$ and a set $W$ of its vertex arrows, write $C[W^{-1}]$ for enriched localization: the derived pushout that adjoins an inverse to each $w\in W$, namely the homotopy pushout of $C\leftarrow\coprod_{w\in W}[1]\to\coprod_{w\in W}J$, where $[1]$ is the discrete walking arrow and $J$ the discrete groupoid on two objects with one arrow between every ordered pair. This construction is functorial for enriched functors preserving the specified arrows.

If every arrow of $W$ is already invertible in $\pi_0 C$, the canonical functor $C\to C[W^{-1}]$ is a Dwyer--Kan equivalence. If $\mathcal M$ is a combinatorial simplicial model category and $W$ is its weak equivalences between fibrant objects, the canonical enriched functor
$$\mathcal M^{cf}\longrightarrow\mathcal M^f[W^{-1}]$$
is a Dwyer--Kan equivalence. The superscripts denote the full enriched subcategories of bifibrant and fibrant objects, with their actual enriched mapping sets. This comparison commutes with enriched functors preserving bifibrant objects, fibrant objects and weak equivalences. A functor preserving only fibrant objects and their weak equivalences still induces a functor between the localized fibrant categories; no functor on bifibrant subcategories is asserted in that case.

Let $H:J\to\mathrm{sCat}$ be any small diagram and let $\alpha:C\to\lim_J H$ be an enriched cone. Suppose an enriched functor $\beta:B\to C$ makes $\alpha\beta$ exhibit $B$ as a homotopy limit of $H$. Then $\alpha$ exhibits $C$ as a homotopy limit if and only if for every $x,y\in C$ its cone on mapping simplicial sets exhibits
$$C(x,y)\simeq\operatorname{holim}_{j\in J}H(j)(\alpha_jx,\alpha_jy).$$
In particular, mapping sets in a homotopy limit have this description. A strict inverse limit of a sequence of Kan fibrations between Kan complexes computes the homotopy limit of the sequence. None of these assertions assumes the coherent-nerve comparison theorem or a model structure on a slice of simplicial sets.

source.place: Notation A.3.5.1; Remark A.3.2.14 and Example A.3.2.18 (localization at equivalences); Proposition A.3.2.27 and Corollary A.3.2.28, printed p.869; Lemma A.3.6.17, printed p.904, applied after universe enlargement. Kan-tower computation is the inverse Reedy model calculation. Read online; archival HTT WANTED; no Stacks tag.

proof.text: First construct the required Dwyer--Kan model structure without coherent nerves. In the notation of [lem-coef-simplicial-interval-lifting], $I$-injective functors are exactly functors surjective on objects and trivial Kan fibrations on every mapping set: test $\varnothing\to\{0\}$ and the maps $U(\partial\Delta^n)\to U(\Delta^n)$. These are exactly the Dwyer--Kan equivalences that are $J$-injective. For the reverse inclusion, essential surjectivity followed by the equivalence-lifting property of $J$-injectives gives actual surjectivity on objects, and local weak equivalences that are Kan fibrations are trivial fibrations. For the forward inclusion, lift the target object by object-surjectivity and the desired vertex by the local trivial fibration; full faithfulness on $\pi_0$ makes that lift invertible. The two small-object weak factorization systems exist by the same node. Every $J$-cofibration is an $I$-cofibration and a weak equivalence by the retract description and [lem-coef-simplicial-interval-cell-stability]. If an $I$-cofibration is a weak equivalence, factor it as a $J$-cofibration followed by a $J$-injective map; two-out-of-three makes the latter $I$-injective, so the lifting/retract argument makes the original map $J$-cofibrant. This proves both lifting axioms. Completeness, cocompleteness and local presentability are supplied by the interval-lifting node; the generating sets give combinatoriality. Fibrant objects have Kan mapping sets, and the stated description of fibrations follows from the explicit $J$-injective test.

source.place: Theorem A.3.2.24 and simplicial-set case Example A.3.2.18; Bergner generating-family recognition, using the two existing interval nodes

proof.text: Use the homotopy mapping property of [lem-coef-simplicial-inversion-universal-property]. If every $w$ is already invertible in $\pi_0C$, every homotopy class $C\to T$ inverts $W$. Thus $1_C:C\to C$ satisfies precisely the same homotopy mapping property as $C\to L_WC$. Uniqueness gives an isomorphism under $C$ in the model homotopy category, hence $C\to L_WC$ is a Dwyer--Kan equivalence. Here and below the elementary model Whitehead argument can be used to detect this: after cofibrant-fibrant replacement, an isomorphism has representatives inverse up to model homotopy. The endpoints of a cylinder are weak equivalences by two-out-of-three with its weak-equivalence projection. If one endpoint composite of a homotopy is a weak equivalence, two-out-of-three makes the homotopy map and its other endpoint composite weak equivalences. Apply this to both composites of the inverse representatives. For Dwyer--Kan equivalences, two-out-of-six follows from two-out-of-six for equivalences of ordinary categories and weak homotopy equivalences of mapping spaces, transporting endpoints along the component-category equivalences. This yields the asserted weak equivalence of the original map.

source.place: Notation A.3.5.1 and Proposition A.3.5.5, with the localization-at-equivalences argument of Lemma A.3.6.17

proof.text: Construct a simplicially enriched cofibrant replacement $Q\xrightarrow{q}1_{\mathcal M}$ by applying [lem-coef-enriched-functorial-factorizations] to $\varnothing\to X$ with the generating cofibrations of $\mathcal M$. Its tensor hypothesis holds: for every simplicial set $K$ and cofibration $i$, $K\otimes i$ is the pushout product of $\varnothing\to K$ and $i$, hence a cofibration by the simplicial model axiom of [lem-coef-simplicial-projective-model-calculus]. For fibrant $X$, the trivial fibration $q_X:QX\to X$ makes $QX$ fibrant as well as cofibrant. Naturality and two-out-of-three imply that $Q$ preserves weak equivalences. Also every weak equivalence $f:X\to Y$ between bifibrant objects is invertible in $\pi_0\mathcal M^{cf}$. Explicitly factor it as a trivial cofibration $i:X\to Z$ followed by a trivial fibration $p:Z\to Y$; $Z$ is bifibrant. Lifting gives $r:Z\to X$ with $ri=1$ and $s:Y\to Z$ with $ps=1$. SM7 gives trivial fibrations $i^*:\operatorname{Map}(Z,Z)\to\operatorname{Map}(X,Z)$ and $p_*:\operatorname{Map}(Z,Z)\to\operatorname{Map}(Z,Y)$. Their fibers connect $ir$ to $1_Z$ and $sp$ to $1_Z$, respectively. Therefore $rs$ is an inverse to $f=pi$ in the category of components.

source.place: Lemma A.3.6.17, enriched cofibrant replacement and the bifibrant weak-equivalence assertion; enriched factorization hypothesis checked explicitly

proof.text: Let $A$ be a simplicial category with marked vertex arrows $V$, and let $\eta:F_0\to F_1$ be an enriched transformation of functors $A\to B$. Suppose both functors send $V$ into a set $W$ of arrows of $B$ and all components of $\eta$ lie in $W$. Enriched naturality defines a functor $h:A\times[1]\to B$ inverting, after localization in $B$, the horizontal and vertical set $U$ of [lem-coef-simplicial-marked-cylinder-comparison]. The essential-surjectivity hypothesis of that lemma holds for $A\to L_VA$ by [lem-coef-simplicial-localization-essential-image]. Thus it identifies $L_U(A\times[1])$ with $(L_VA)\times\mathbb J$, carrying the localized endpoint maps to its two endpoint inclusions. Projection to $L_VA$ is a Dwyer--Kan equivalence: its maps on mapping sets are isomorphisms, and every object is isomorphic to one at either endpoint. Both endpoint inclusions are therefore its same inverse in $h\mathrm{sCat}$. By [lem-coef-simplicial-inversion-universal-property], $h$ induces a morphism from the localized cylinder to $L_WB$; its restrictions are $L F_0$ and $L F_1$. Equality of the endpoint maps gives $[L F_0]=[L F_1]$.

source.place: Proof of Lemma A.3.6.17, interval localization; Lemma A.3.5.14

proof.text: Put $G=W\cap\mathcal M^{cf}$. Inclusion $i:\mathcal M^{cf}\to\mathcal M^f$ and the restriction of $Q$ induce $\bar i:L_G\mathcal M^{cf}\to L_W\mathcal M^f$ and $\bar Q$ in the opposite direction. Apply step 4 to $q:iQ\to1_{\mathcal M^f}$ and to its restriction $Qi\to1_{\mathcal M^{cf}}$. All components and all images of marked arrows are weak equivalences by step 3. It follows that $\bar i\bar Q=1$ and $\bar Q\bar i=1$ in $h\mathrm{sCat}$. Choose cofibrant--fibrant replacements of the source and target of $\bar i$; the inverse equality supplies representatives in both directions whose composites are cylinder-homotopic to the identities. The cylinder projections are weak equivalences, so two-out-of-three makes both composites and then the representatives themselves Dwyer--Kan equivalences; hence $\bar i$ is a Dwyer--Kan equivalence. By step 3 all arrows of $G$ are already invertible in $\pi_0\mathcal M^{cf}$, so step 2 gives $\mathcal M^{cf}\xrightarrow{\sim}L_G\mathcal M^{cf}$. Its composite with $\bar i$ is exactly the canonical comparison in the item, proving that comparison is a Dwyer--Kan equivalence.

source.place: Lemma A.3.6.17, applied to the entire model category after universe enlargement; no chunk or coherent-nerve theorem is needed

proof.text: For an enriched functor $T:\mathcal M\to\mathcal N$ preserving fibrant objects and their weak equivalences, the functor of relative simplicial categories $(\mathcal M^f,W_{\mathcal M})\to(\mathcal N^f,W_{\mathcal N})$ induces a map on the chosen functorial derived pushouts. If $T$ also preserves bifibrant objects, its restriction gives the other side of the comparison square. Both composites are induced from the same enriched functor $\mathcal M^{cf}\to\mathcal N^f$ followed by localization, so the square commutes, using functorial choices (and in the derived category independently of those choices). No compatibility of $T$ with $Q$ was used: $Q$ proved invertibility of the comparison, while the comparison itself was inclusion followed by localization.

source.place: Functoriality of Notation A.3.5.1 and Lemma A.3.6.17

proof.text: Apply [lem-coef-combinatorial-injective-diagram-model] to the combinatorial model structure of step 1 and the small ordinary diagram $H$. Choose $H\xrightarrow{\sim}RH$ injectively fibrant and put $L=\lim_J RH$. The given cone induces $a:C\to L$. A cone is homotopy limiting exactly when its comparison to $L$ is a Dwyer--Kan equivalence. This includes the comparison $a\beta:B\to L$, which is a Dwyer--Kan equivalence by the hypothesis on $\alpha\beta$. We will compute the mapping sets of $L$ directly, rather than appeal to coherent nerves.

source.place: Proposition A.3.2.27 and Corollary A.3.2.28, first reduction to an injectively fibrant diagram

proof.text:
Fix two strictly compatible systems of objects $x_j,y_j$ in $RH$. The mapping diagram $M(j)=RH(j)(x_j,y_j)$ is injectively fibrant as a diagram of simplicial sets. Indeed, for any objectwise trivial cofibration $T\to T'$ of such diagrams, form the two-object simplicial-category diagrams $U(T)\to U(T')$, keeping the two labelled objects and identity maps in every degree. Objectwise this is a trivial cofibration for the model structure of step 1: it is locally a weak equivalence and identity on objects, and has the left lifting property against the object-surjective local trivial fibrations by the simplicial-set lifting property. Thus it is an injective trivial cofibration. The prescribed map $T\to M$ and the prescribed endpoint systems define $U(T)\to RH$; injective fibrancy lifts it to $U(T')\to RH$. Because the object maps in $U(T)\to U(T')$ are identities, the lift retains the endpoint systems, giving the desired lift $T'\to M$. Consequently $M$ is injectively fibrant. Strict limits of enriched categories compute mapping sets at compatible objects as strict limits, by the defining equalities for objects, arrows and composition. Hence
$$L(x,y)=\lim_j RH(j)(x_j,y_j)\simeq\operatorname{holim}_j RH(j)(x_j,y_j).$$

source.place: Proposition A.3.2.27, walking-arrow lifting proof, printed p.869

proof.text: For the endpoints coming from $c,d\in C$, each map $H(j)(\alpha_jc,\alpha_jd)\to RH(j)(\alpha_jc,\alpha_jd)$ is a weak homotopy equivalence, because $H(j)\to RH(j)$ is a Dwyer--Kan equivalence. Therefore replacing this diagram by the latter does not change its derived limit. By step 8, the displayed condition on the mapping cones of $\alpha$ is equivalent to $a:C\to L$ being a weak homotopy equivalence on every mapping set. If $a$ is a Dwyer--Kan equivalence this holds, proving necessity and also the mapping-set description for any homotopy-limiting cone, without the auxiliary $\beta$. Conversely, if it holds then $\pi_0a$ is fully faithful. For any object $l$ of $L$, essential surjectivity of $\pi_0(a\beta)$ gives $b\in B$ with $a\beta b\cong l$ in $\pi_0L$; thus $a$ is also essentially surjective. It is a Dwyer--Kan equivalence, so $\alpha$ is homotopy limiting by step 7.

source.place: Corollary A.3.2.28, using Proposition A.3.2.27; fully faithful plus essential-surjectivity argument

proof.text: For the final tower assertion, give $\mathbb N^{\mathrm{op}}$ its inverse Reedy structure with degree $n$. All latching categories are empty. The matching object is terminal at $0$ and is $X_{n-1}$ at $n>0$, since the category of nonidentity arrows from $n$ has initial object $n\to n-1$. Thus a tower of Kan complexes whose successive maps are Kan fibrations is Reedy fibrant by [lem-coef-reedy-model-structure]. The constant diagram functor preserves cofibrations and trivial cofibrations: with empty latching categories the Reedy cofibration test is exactly the ground cofibration test in each degree. Its right adjoint $\lim$ is right Quillen; evaluating its right derived functor at this already fibrant tower gives precisely its strict limit. This proves the stated weak equivalence to the homotopy limit. It agrees with the homotopy limit defined through an injectively fibrant replacement in [lem-coef-combinatorial-injective-diagram-model]: the Reedy and injective structures on towers have the same weak equivalences and $\lim$ is right Quillen for both, so both compute the total right derived functor of $\lim$, which depends only on the weak equivalences; concretely, an injectively fibrant replacement of the Reedy fibrant tower is an objectwise weak equivalence between Reedy fibrant towers, which the right Quillen functor $\lim$ carries to a weak equivalence. Its limit is Kan since the right Quillen functor carries fibrant objects to fibrant objects. The argument also works for empty mapping complexes and requires no surjectivity on vertices.

source.place: Inverse Reedy model calculation for the Kan tower; compare HTT Lemma 5.3.4.11 only for this space-valued assertion
